reason: A five-word run and the second-ranked candidate in the verse, and both halves are boilerplate. Leviticus 24:23 is Moses ordering the blasphemer taken out of the camp and stoned; 3 Nephi 18:1 is Jesus asking for bread and wine. ‘Commanded … that they should bring forth’ is the KJV’s ordinary syntax for a relayed order and the Book of Mormon uses it continuously. The first-ranked candidate in the same verse, Matthew 16:20 (‘his disciples that they should’), is the same phenomenon and is covered here rather than listed twice; it recurs at 18:8 for the same reason.

The top-scoring candidate in the verse and it is the machine reading syntax as content. Matthew 27:20 is the chief priests persuading the crowd to ask for Barabbas and destroy Jesus; 3 Nephi 18:2 is Jesus seating a crowd for a meal. The four shared words are ‘the multitude that they should’, which is simply how the KJV introduces an instruction given to a crowd. The real source of this verse is the feeding-miracle seating formula — “commanded the multitude to sit down” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 14:19 and Matthew 15:35 — and the link is filed there. Worth an entry because the machine ranked a Passion verse first in the chapter that institutes the sacrament, which is exactly the trap CONVENTIONS §9 describes.

“the gates of hell” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 16:18, so the candidate is as rare as candidates get, and the borrowing is real — but it is not first made here. 3 Nephi 11:39-40 has already welded Matthew 16:18 to Matthew 7:24-27 in almost these words: ‘whoso buildeth upon this, buildeth upon my rock; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against them … is not built upon my rock, but he buildeth upon a sandy foundation, and the gates of hell standeth open to receive such, when the floods come, and the winds beat upon them.’ 18:12-13 is that sentence again, and Matthew 16:18 is adjudicated at 3 Nephi 11:39 (see also 3 Nephi 11:40 for Matthew 7:26). A reader who arrives at 18:13 should be sent there. What remains fresh at 18:13 — the restored ‘rain’, which 11:40 dropped and Matthew 7:25/27 has — carries the link written at this verse to Matthew 7:27, and discharges Hardy’s cross-reference. Note also the 1830 reading, ‘the gates of hell is already open to receive them’, with a singular verb and ‘already’ for ‘ready’; 1920 prints ‘the gates of hell are ready to receive them’.

A six-word run and the only candidate the machine offered in this verse, and it is as opposed in sense as a match can be. Ezekiel 16:33 is the prophet’s figure of Jerusalem as a whore who pays her lovers ‘that they may come unto thee on every side for thy whoredom’; 3 Nephi 18:22 forbids the disciples to turn anyone away from the assembly. Nothing is shared but the infinitive of approach. The verse’s actual source is the Synoptic children saying — “forbid them not” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Matthew 19:14, Mark 10:14 and Luke 18:16 — and the link is filed at 18:22 accordingly.

‘Hold up your light, that it may shine unto the world’ is the Sermon’s lamp saying, and “let your light so shine” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 5:16 — but 3 Nephi has already transcribed that verse in full at 12:16, where it is adjudicated as a certain quotation. 18:24 is the same speaker citing his own earlier sermon back to the same audience, which is the recurrence case of ADJUDICATING §4 and not a fresh borrowing. The same applies to ‘Behold I am the light which ye shall hold up’: “I am the light” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 8:12 and John 9:5, and John 8:12 is already adjudicated at 3 Nephi 9:18 and 11:11. Both belong here as cross-references rather than as rows. What is genuinely new at 18:24 — ‘hold up’, which is in no KJV verse in this sense — is the Book of Mormon’s own contribution and cannot be catalogued as dependence.

sharedText: what ye have seen me do
reason: The best entry in this register and it has to be written out, because a reader who finds it will assume the catalogue missed it. “ye have seen me do” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, and the other one is Abimelech at mount Zalmon: he cuts a bough, lays it on his shoulder, and tells his men ‘What ye have seen me do, make haste, and do as I have done’ — after which they pile boughs against the tower of Shechem and burn a thousand men and women alive inside it (Judges 9:49). 3 Nephi 18:24 reads ‘Behold I am the light which ye shall hold up — that which ye have seen me do.’ The formula is identical, the situation is a leader making his own performed act the pattern for his followers, and the outcomes are a massacre and a lamp. The rarity is real and the coincidence is a coincidence: nothing else in Judges 9 is present, and the Book of Mormon’s sentence has a much closer home in John 13:15 (“I have given you an example” occurs in exactly one KJV verse), which is filed as the link at 18:16.

sharedText: When Jesus had spoken these words
reason: A four-word run reproducing a KJV singleton exactly — “When Jesus had spoken these words” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 18:1 — and it is still boilerplate, because the Book of Mormon has made it boilerplate. The phrase appears six times in the 1830 text, all of them in this one visit: 3 Nephi 12:1, 13:25, 14:1, 15:11, 17:1 and 18:26, where it marks each turn of the discourse from one audience to another. A formula the narrator uses six times in seven chapters is his transition device, not a borrowing from the verse that happens to share it; John 18:1’s own continuation is Jesus crossing the Cedron into Gethsemane, which has nothing to do with any of the six. The entry is written rather than passed over in silence because the KJV rarity is genuine and will keep re-ranking this candidate.

The Isaiah 6:10 healing formula, in its New Testament rather than its Old Testament form, and it is adjudicated at 3 Nephi 9:13 rather than here. `mediation-check.py` run on this verse against Isaiah 6:10 and Matthew 13:15 returns one decisive point — the Book of Mormon has the New Testament’s ‘I should heal them’, a first-person divine healer, against Isaiah’s agentless ‘be healed’ — so the mediation is settled and it is settled the same way it was at 9:13, which has the fuller sentence (‘return unto me, and repent of your sins, and be converted, that I may heal you’) and the second decisive divergence as well. 18:32’s ‘they will return and repent, and come unto me … and I shall heal them’ is the same speaker’s same formula nine chapters later, which is the recurrence case of ADJUDICATING §4. Note one caution about the tool at this verse: its ‘backbone’ of shared words (heart, ears, eyes, lest, see, hear, understand) is computed between the two candidates and not against the Book of Mormon, and 18:32 has almost none of them — the decisive point stands, the backbone does not corroborate it here.

“return and repent” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Joel 2:14, which is why the machine ranked it, and the rarity is arithmetic rather than distinctive: the two verbs are the standard KJV pair for turning back to God and the Bible simply had occasion to put them in this order once. Joel 2:14 is a question about whether the LORD will relent and leave a grain offering behind him — ‘Who knoweth if he will return and repent’, where the subject of both verbs is God and ‘repent’ means to change a purpose. 3 Nephi 18:32’s subject is an excommunicated man and ‘repent’ means contrition. Same two words, opposite grammatical subject, opposite sense of the second verb.

A five-word run split across a clause boundary in Jude and therefore meaningless. Jude 1:10 reads ‘these speak evil of those things which they know not: but what they know naturally, as brute beasts’ — the machine’s window has closed over the colon, joining the end of one clause to the start of the next. 3 Nephi 18:32’s ‘ye know not but what they will return and repent’ is a single idiom for uncertainty. This is the trap ADJUDICATING §4 calls the window closing one word early, in its other form: the window opening one clause too soon.

The top-ranked candidate in the verse, on the strength of ‘and it came to pass, when Jesus had made an end of’, and it is two formulas in a row. “made an end of” occurs in exactly thirty-eight KJV verses and is the King James Bible’s standard way of closing a speech or a task; the Book of Mormon uses it throughout. Matthew 11:1’s own continuation — Jesus departing to teach and preach in the cities — has nothing to do with 3 Nephi 18:36, where he touches the twelve one by one and confers the Holy Ghost. Two nearer candidates exist and neither carries: Matthew 7:28, where “ended these sayings” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, is the wrong verb, and Genesis 49:33, the only other verse with ‘made an end of commanding’, is Jacob dying. The verse’s real content is the laying on of hands, filed as a link at 18:37 against Acts 8:17-19.

“he departed from them” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 19:9, and the verse is Paul withdrawing from the synagogue at Ephesus because ‘divers were hardened, and believed not, but spake evil of that way’, taking the disciples off to the school of Tyrannus. 3 Nephi 18:39 is the Ascension. The shared words are the plainest English for leaving a group and the senses are opposed — Acts 19:9 is a separation caused by unbelief and followed by two more years of teaching; 18:39 is a departure into heaven witnessed by believers. The verse’s genuine sources are registered with the link at 18:38: “a cloud received him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 1:9, and “carried up into heaven” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 24:51.
